sections.title: Radiation Protection, Contrast Safety and Physics

modules.title: Pediatric Radiation Protection, ALARA and Contrast Media

lessonTopics.title: Image Gently Campaign: ALARA Principles and Pediatric CT Optimization
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Physics & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: The Image Gently campaign promotes child-sizing of radiation exposure by tailoring CT scan parameters (kVp, mAs, pitch) strictly to patient weight and diameter.
mustKnow.source: Image Gently / Alliance for Radiation Safety

mustKnow.fact: Size-Specific Dose Estimate (SSDE) adjusts volume CT dose index (CTDIvol) based on the patient's effective cross-sectional diameter, providing accurate organ dose estimation in children.
Routine unenhanced (non-contrast) or multiphase scanning is eliminated in pediatric body CT, reducing lifetime attributable cancer risk by 50-70%.
Reducing tube potential from 120 kVp to 70-80 kVp in infants increases photoelectric absorption of iodine, dramatically improving contrast conspicuity at substantially reduced radiation.
Model-based and deep-learning iterative reconstruction software allows 40-60% reduction in radiation dose while maintaining diagnostic signal-to-noise ratio.
Ultrasound is the mandatory first-line imaging modality for pediatric abdominal pain, palpable mass, suspected appendicitis, intussusception, and neonatal head imaging, with zero ionizing radiation.
Pediatric fluoroscopic examinations (voiding cystourethrogram, upper GI series) utilize low pulsed rates (3-7.5 pulses per second) and grid removal in infants under 10 kg.
Pediatric tissues exhibit a 3 to 10-fold higher lifetime radiation sensitivity compared to adults due to rapid cellular mitotic proliferation and longer life expectancy.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Intravenous Contrast Agents and Sedation Protocols
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Contrast & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Low-osmolar non-ionic monomers (iohexol, iopamidol) are standard for pediatric IV contrast, administered at 1.5 to 2.0 mL/kg (maximum 3.0 mL/kg or 100 mL total).
Macrocyclic gadolinium-based contrast agents (gadobutrol, gadoterate) with high thermodynamic stability are preferred in children to eliminate risk of intracranial and bone gadolinium retention.
Linear gadolinium contrast agents are suspended or severely restricted in pediatric patients due to documented long-term deposition in the dentate nucleus and globus pallidus.
Renal function in children is calculated using the updated Bedside Schwartz formula: eGFR = 0.413 x Height (cm) / Serum Creatinine (mg/dL).
NSF is virtually eliminated when eGFR exceeds 30 mL/min/1.73m2 and macrocyclic agents are employed at standard dose (0.1 mmol/kg / 0.2 mL/kg).

Water-soluble iodinated contrast (Gastrografin / meglumine diatrizoate) is hyperosmolar (1900 mOsm/L) and must be diluted 1:4 to 1:5 in neonates to prevent fluid shift, hypovolemia, and enterocolitis.
The feed and swaddle immobilization technique achieves diagnostic quality brain and spine MRI in infants under 3-4 months of age without general anesthesia in over 85-90% of scans.
Peripheral IV contrast extravasation in neonates requires immediate catheter removal, extremity elevation, cold compress application, and plastic surgery consult if volume exceeds 5-10 mL.

modules.title: Neonatal Cranial Ultrasound and Periventricular Injury

lessonTopics.title: Germinal Matrix Hemorrhage: Papile Classification and Complications
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Neuro & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: The subependymal germinal matrix at the caudothalamic groove is a highly cellular, fragile, vascularized layer that regresses by 32-34 weeks gestation, predisposing premature infants to hemorrhage.
Grade I hemorrhage is confined entirely to the subependymal germinal matrix at the caudothalamic notch without ventricular extension.
Grade II hemorrhage extends into the lateral ventricle filling less than 50% of the ventricular lumen without causing ventricular dilatation.
Grade III hemorrhage fills more than 50% of the lateral ventricle and is associated with acute ventricular dilatation.
Grade IV (periventricular venous hemorrhagic infarction) is not a true extension but a secondary hemorrhagic venous infarction caused by obstruction of the terminal medullary veins.
Routine screening cranial ultrasound in very low birth weight infants (< 1500 g or < 30 weeks) is performed between day 3 and 7 of life, with over 90% of GMH occurring by day 3.
Ventricular enlargement occurs from obliterative arachnoiditis or blood clots obstructing the aqueduct of Sylvius, tracked by ventricular index (Levene curve).
The mastoid (posterolateral) fontanelle view allows high-resolution acoustic visualization of fourth ventricular hemorrhage, cerebellar hemispheres, and cisterna magna.

lessonTopics.title: Periventricular Leukomalacia (PVL) and Neonatal HIE Imaging
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Neuro & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Periventricular leukomalacia affects the periventricular white matter adjacent to the trigone of lateral ventricles and frontal horns (watershed of deep penetrating arteries).
Acute phase (days 1-7) shows increased echogenicity brighter than the choroid plexus; cystic degeneration (cystic PVL) emerges at 2 to 4 weeks post-insult.
PVL selectively injures descending corticospinal motor tracts supplying the lower extremities, resulting in spastic diplegia or quadriplegia.
Acute profound asphyxia in term neonates selectively damages metabolically active deep gray nuclei: ventrolateral thalami and posterior putamina in a symmetrical distribution.

mustKnow.term: Absent PLIC sign on T1 MRI
mustKnow.fact: Loss of the normal hyperintense T1 myelin signal in the posterior limb of the internal capsule (PLIC sign) in term infants predicts adverse motor outcome and cerebral palsy with > 90% sensitivity.
Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) demonstrates cytotoxic edema with restricted diffusion (low ADC) that peaks between days 3 and 5 of life, followed by pseudonormalization by day 7-10.
Partial prolonged asphyxia in term neonates injures the cortical and subcortical watershed border zones between anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries.
Therapeutic whole-body hypothermia (33.5 degrees C for 72 hours) alters the timeline of MRI signal changes, making day 4-7 the optimal neuroimaging window.

lessonTopics.title: Craniosynostosis and Skull Sutural Pathology
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Neuro & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Premature fusion of the sagittal suture (scaphocephaly / dolichocephaly) is the most common craniosynostosis (50-60%), resulting in an elongated, boat-shaped calvarium.
Unilateral coronal synostosis (plagiocephaly) elevates the ipsilateral sphenoid ridge and superior orbital rim, producing the pathognomonic Harlequin eye sign.
Premature closure of the metopic suture creates trigonocephaly, characterized by a pointed triangular forehead, hypotelorism, and prominent midline frontal keel.

Positional non-synostotic plagiocephaly produces a parallelogram skull shape with ipsilateral frontal bossing, whereas true lambdoid synostosis creates a trapezoid skull with ipsilateral ear displacement downward and backward.
Kleeblattschadel (cloverleaf skull) results from pan-synostosis of coronal, lambdoid, and sagittal sutures, classically associated with Thanatophoric dysplasia Type 2 and Pfeiffer syndrome.
Diffuse inner calvarial table convolutional indentations (beaten brass / copper-beaten skull) reflect chronically elevated intracranial pressure in multi-suture synostosis.
Volumetric 3D surface-rendered low-dose CT provides the definitive preoperative roadmap for skull vault remodeling, assessing suture patency and intracranial volume.
Apert, Crouzon, and Pfeiffer syndromes are autosomal dominant conditions driven by gain-of-function mutations in FGFR2 or FGFR3, featuring midface hypoplasia and complex synostosis.

lessonTopics.title: Spinal Dysraphism and Tethered Cord Syndrome
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Spine & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: The normal conus medullaris tip terminates above the lower border of L2 in term neonates (at L1-L2 by 3 months); termination at L3 or lower defines a low-lying/tethered cord.
A filum terminale diameter exceeding 2.0 mm measured on axial T1 MRI at the L5-S1 level defines abnormal thickening in tethered cord syndrome.
Open spinal dysraphism (myelomeningocele) lacks cutaneous coverage, exposes neural placode, and is universally associated with Chiari II malformation and elevated maternal AFP.
Closed spinal dysraphism with a subcutaneous mass: lipomyelomeningocele extends through a posterior vertebral defect, with the neural-lipoma junction lying outside the spinal canal.
Split cord malformation (diastematomyelia) features sagittal division of the spinal cord into two hemicords; Type I has separate dural sacs divided by an osseous or cartilaginous spur.
A dermal sinus tract is an epithelium-lined tube extending from a cutaneous midline pit above the gluteal crease inward to the thecal sac, posing high risk of recurrent meningitis.
Spinal ultrasonography is the primary screening modality for sacral dimples in infants under 3-4 months before posterior vertebral arches fully ossify.
Maternal gestational diabetes is the primary risk factor for caudal regression syndrome, featuring sacral agenesis, clubfeet, and a blunt wedge-shaped conus ending high at T11-T12.

modules.title: Posterior Fossa Anomalies, Dysraphism and Brain Tumors

lessonTopics.title: Dandy-Walker, Joubert, Chiari and Posterior Fossa Malformations
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Neuro & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Dandy-Walker malformation classical triad: agenesis/hypoplasia of cerebellar vermis, cystic dilation of fourth ventricle filling posterior fossa, and high confluence of sinuses (torcular-lambdoid inversion).
Blake pouch cyst features an enlarged retrocerebellar fluid space from failed fenestration of the foramen of Magendie, with a completely normal vermis and non-enlarged posterior fossa.
Mega cisterna magna is defined by retrocerebellar CSF space > 10 mm on midline sagittal imaging with intact cerebellar vermis, normal fourth ventricle, and no hydrocephalus.
Chiari II features a small posterior fossa, downward herniation of inferior vermis and medulla through foramen magnum, beaked tectum, and 100% association with lumbar myelomeningocele.

Joubert syndrome pathognomonic MRI sign is the molar tooth sign, caused by cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, deepened interpeduncular fossa, and elongated, thickened, non-decussating superior cerebellar peduncles.
Rhombencephalosynapsis is characterized by complete or partial absence of the cerebellar vermis with fusion of the cerebellar hemispheres across the midline and a keyhole-shaped fourth ventricle.
Alobar holoprosencephaly features complete non-separation of cerebral hemispheres with a monoventricle and fused thalami, strongly associated with facial anomalies and Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) mutations.
Type 1 lissencephaly (LIS1 gene, Miller-Dieker syndrome) shows a smooth brain surface with thickened 4-layered cortex and figure-of-8 hour-glass configuration on axial imaging.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Brain Tumors: Infratentorial and Supratentorial Neoplasms
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Neuro & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: In children aged 1 to 10 years, over 60-70% of primary intracranial tumors are infratentorial (posterior fossa), flipping to supratentorial in neonates and adolescents.
Medulloblastoma (WHO grade 4) arises from the cerebellar vermis roof of the 4th ventricle, shows high cellularity with hyperdensity on CT, and marked diffusion restriction (low ADC) on DWI.
All medulloblastoma patients require whole-neuroaxis contrast-enhanced spine MRI before surgery to detect leptomeningeal drop metastases (present in up to 30%).
Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade 1) is characteristically a cystic lesion with an intensely enhancing mural nodule located in the cerebellar hemisphere, demonstrating low cellularity and high ADC.
Infratentorial ependymoma (WHO grade 2-3) arises from the floor of the 4th ventricle, extends through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie (plastic / squeeze tumor), and calcifies in > 50%.
Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (H3 K27M-mutant) expands the pons, engulfs the basilar artery posteriorly, displays T2 hyperintensity, and typically lacks prominent enhancement on presentation.
Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma follows the 90% rule: 90% cystic, 90% calcified, and 90% enhancing, presenting as a suprasellar lobulated mass.
Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor (ATRT) occurs in children under 3 years with SMARCB1/INI1 loss, exhibiting more necrosis, hemorrhage, and off-midline cerebellopontine angle location.

lessonTopics.title: Neurocutaneous Syndromes: NF1, Tuberous Sclerosis and Sturge-Weber
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Neuro & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1 / von Recklinghausen) features optic pathway gliomas (15-20%), focal areas of signal intensity (FASI / unidentified bright objects on T2), sphenoid wing dysplasia, and plexiform neurofibromas.

Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC1/TSC2) demonstrates subependymal nodules (candle guttering calcifying along lateral ventricles), cortical/subcortical tubers, and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGA).
SEGA arises near the foramen of Monro, showing serial growth and intense contrast enhancement, causing obstructive hydrocephalus; treated with surgical resection or mTOR inhibitors (everolimus).

Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) displays unilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis, ipsilateral choroid plexus enlargement, and tram-track gyriform cortical calcifications on CT.
Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2 / MISME syndrome) is defined by bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas), multiple intracranial meningiomas, and spinal ependymomas.
VHL syndrome features cerebellar and spinal cord hemangioblastomas (cystic mass with intensely enhancing mural nodule abutting pial surface) associated with retinal angiomas and clear cell RCC.
ATM gene mutation causes progressive cerebellar vermian and hemisphere atrophy, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and systemic telangiectasias, with heightened radiosensitivity.
Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (PTCH1 mutation) features odontogenic keratocysts of the jaw, falx cerebri calcification, bifid ribs, and medulloblastoma.

lessonTopics.title: Congenital TORCH Infections and Neonatal Brain Calcifications
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Neuro & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Congenital Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common intrauterine viral infection, classically showing extensive periventricular calcifications, polymicrogyria, white matter T2 hyperintensity, and sensorineural deafness.

Congenital toxoplasmosis produces randomly scattered diffuse nodular parenchymal calcifications throughout the cortex, basal ganglia, and subcortical white matter, alongside hydrocephalus and chorioretinitis.
Neonatal Herpes Simplex Virus type 2 (HSV-2) causes diffuse, catastrophic multicystic encephalomalacia with prominent temporal and frontal lobe predilection and cortical diffusion restriction.
Congenital rubella syndrome features subependymal cysts, basal ganglia vasculopathy (branching striatocerebral calcifications), microcephaly, and cataracts.

Congenital Zika virus infection produces severe fetal brain disruption sequence: extreme microcephaly, redundant scalp rugae, thin cerebral cortex with subcortical band calcifications at gray-white junction, and ventriculomegaly.

Echogenic branching streaks in the basal ganglia on neonatal cranial ultrasound (lenticulostriate vasculopathy) reflect mineralizing microangiopathy from TORCH infection, trisomy 21, or hypoxic insult.

Connatal cysts are normal developmental variants at the superolateral angle of the frontal horns; true subependymal cysts are post-hemorrhagic or post-infectious lesions located posterior to the caudothalamic groove.
Hydranencephaly results from bilateral internal carotid artery occlusion in utero, sparing the posterior fossa, thalami, and brainstem (supplied by intact posterior circulation / basilar artery).

modules.title: Neonatal Respiratory Distress and Congenital Thoracic Pathology

lessonTopics.title: Neonatal Respiratory Distress: RDS, TTN, MAS and Air Leak
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Chest & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Respiratory distress syndrome (surfactant deficiency in preterm < 32 weeks) shows low lung volume (bell-shaped thorax), diffuse symmetrical reticulogranular opacities, and air bronchograms.
Transient tachypnea of the newborn in near-term/Cesarean deliveries displays normal to hyperinflated lung volumes, perihilar streaky interstitial markings, and fluid in the horizontal minor fissure.
Meconium aspiration syndrome in term/post-term neonates presents with asymmetric coarse ropy infiltrates, hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms, and pneumothorax in 20-30%.
Pneumomediastinum elevates and displaces the thymic lobes laterally, creating the pathognomonic angel wing or spinnaker-sail sign on neonatal AP chest radiograph.

mustKnow.term: Deep sulcus sign in supine neonate
mustKnow.fact: In a supine neonate, pneumothorax manifests as deepening and lucency of the ipsilateral costophrenic sulcus (deep sulcus sign) or sharp delineation of the hemidiaphragm and cardiac border.
PIE in ventilated premature infants appears as linear and small cystic branching radiolucencies tracking along bronchovascular bundles, caused by alveolar rupture into the interstitium.
Ideal tip position of the endotracheal tube on neonatal radiograph is at the mid-trachea between vertebral levels T1 and T2, at least 1 cm above the carina.
Umbilical arterial catheter (UAC) high line tip rests at T6-T8 (above celiac axis) and low line at L3-L5; umbilical venous catheter (UVC) traverses ductus venosus to rest at IVC-RA junction (T8-T9).

lessonTopics.title: Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia, CPAM and Sequestration
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Chest & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Bochdalek diaphragmatic hernia is located posterolaterally (85-90% of CDH), occurs on the left side in 80-85%, and presents with mediastinal shift, intrathoracic bowel loops, and scaphoid abdomen.
Morgagni hernia is retrosternal/anterior (5-10% of CDH), predominantly right-sided, frequently containing liver or omentum with low respiratory morbidity.
Congenital Pulmonary Airway Malformation: Type 1 has single or multiple large cysts (2-10 cm); Type 2 has multiple small cysts (< 2 cm, associated with other anomalies); Type 3 is microcystic/solid.
Extralobar bronchopulmonary sequestration has its own distinct visceral pleural envelope, systemic arterial supply from aorta, and systemic venous drainage to azygos/IVC; 80% left-sided.
Intralobar sequestration shares the visceral pleura of the adjacent normal lung, receives systemic arterial supply from aorta, but drains via normal pulmonary veins (95% lower lobes).
CLE involves progressive bronchial cartilage hypoplasia causing dynamic ball-valve hyperinflation of a single pulmonary lobe (left upper lobe 42%, middle lobe 35%), compressing adjacent lung.
Bronchogenic cysts are foregut duplication anomalies most commonly located in the subcarinal or middle mediastinal space, presenting as smooth, well-marginated non-enhancing fluid masses.
DICER1 gene mutations predispose to Type 1 cystic pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB), which mimics Type 1 CPAM on imaging and requires surgical resection.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Upper Airway Emergencies: Croup, Epiglottitis and Stridor
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Chest & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) demonstrates the steeple sign (pencil-point subglottic narrowing) on AP neck radiograph due to symmetrical subglottic mucosal edema.
Acute epiglottitis features the thumbprint sign on lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph, characterized by thickening and rounded swelling of the epiglottis with obliteration of the vallecula.

Normal prevertebral soft tissue thickness on lateral neck radiograph (in true extension on inspiration) should not exceed 100% of the adjacent vertebral body at C2 or the width of a vertebral body at C6.
Bacterial tracheitis (Staphylococcus aureus) displays subglottic narrowing with irregular, ragged tracheal mucosal contours and detached pseudomembranous intraluminal filling defects.
Double aortic arch is the most common symptomatic vascular ring, compressing both trachea and esophagus, producing bilateral indentations on AP and posterior indentation on lateral barium swallow.
In pulmonary artery sling, the aberrant left pulmonary artery arises from the right PA and courses between the trachea and esophagus, causing anterior esophageal indentation.
Organic foreign body aspiration produces dynamic air trapping (hyperlucency and hyperinflation on expiration) with mediastinal shift away from the affected side on decubitus views.
Laryngomalacia is the leading cause of congenital stridor (60-70%), diagnosed definitively by flexible laryngoscopy showing omega-shaped epiglottis and inspiratory inward collapse of arytenoids.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Mediastinal Compartment Masses and Thymic Pathology
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Chest & RDN11

mustKnow.term: Normal thymic wave and sail sign
mustKnow.fact: The normal pediatric thymus creates the sail sign (triangular, sharp lateral margin) and wave sign (scalloped lateral border from anterior rib indentations) without compressing airways.
Anterior mediastinal mass differential: T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma (most common), Teratoma/germ cell tumor, Thymoma/thymic carcinoma (rare in children), and Thyroid ectopic mass.
T-cell lymphoma presents as a rapidly expanding anterior mediastinal mass causing severe tracheobronchial compression, superior vena cava syndrome, and pleural effusion.
Mature cystic teratoma is a well-encapsulated anterior mass containing fat, fluid, and coarse calcifications (bone or tooth fragments) in over 50% of cases.
Over 90% of posterior mediastinal masses in children are neurogenic tumors arising from sympathetic chain (neuroblastoma, ganglioneuroblastoma, ganglioneuroma) or nerve sheath (schwannoma).
Neurogenic tumors can extend through the intervertebral neural foramen into the spinal canal (dumbbell / hourglass lesion), mandating contrast MRI of the spine before surgical resection.
Middle mediastinal lesions encompass lymphoma, tuberculous lymphadenopathy, bronchogenic cysts, and enteric duplication cysts.
Marked thymic enlargement (rebound hyperplasia) occurs within 2 to 9 months following cessation of chemotherapy or severe burn recovery, demonstrating smooth drop-out on chemical shift MRI.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Pneumonia, Round Pneumonia and Parapneumonic Empyema
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Chest & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Round pneumonia presents as a well-circumscribed solitary spherical mass mimicking a tumor on chest radiograph, occurring almost exclusively in children under 8 years due to underdeveloped canals of Lambert and pores of Kohn.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is the single most common causative organism of round pneumonia and lobar consolidations in healthy immunocompetent children.
Chest ultrasonography is superior to CT for characterizing pleural effusions, accurately detecting internal fibrin stranding, loculations, and septations without ionizing radiation.
Loculated complex parapneumonic effusion or frank empyema with thickened pleural peel is treated with intrapleural fibrinolytics (alteplase / dornase alfa) or thoracoscopic debridement (VATS).

Necrotizing pneumonia (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae serotype 19A/3) demonstrates loss of normal parenchymal enhancement with multiple small thin-walled non-enhancing liquefactive cavities without true epithelial lining.

Post-infectious pneumatoceles are thin-walled, air-filled cystic spaces that develop following staphylococcal or pneumococcal pneumonia; benign lesions that resolve spontaneously over weeks to months.

Swyer-James-Macleod syndrome is a post-infectious obliterative bronchiolitis following childhood adenovirus or mycoplasma pneumonia, manifesting as a unilaterally hyperlucent lung with small pulmonary artery and air trapping.
Right middle lobe atelectasis occurs recurrently due to acute angulation of the long narrow RML bronchus surrounded by a complete ring of lymphatic nodes susceptible to extrinsic compression.

lessonTopics.title: Duodenal Atresia, Malrotation and Midgut Volvulus
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric GI & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Duodenal atresia produces the classic double-bubble sign on plain radiograph (gas in stomach and first duodenal bulb) with complete absence of distal bowel gas; 30% have Down syndrome.
On upper GI fluoroscopy, the normal duodenojejunal (DJ) flexure lies to the left of the left pedicle of the vertebral column at or above the level of the duodenal bulb.
Midgut volvulus displays the pathognomonic corkscrew sign on upper GI series as the small bowel twists around the narrow mesentery, causing complete obstruction.
Color Doppler ultrasound demonstrates the whirlpool sign: clockwise spiraling of the superior mesenteric vein (SMV) and mesentery around the superior mesenteric artery (SMA).
Normal anatomy has the SMV to the right of the SMA; reversal with SMV located to the left or directly anterior to the SMA strongly indicates intestinal malrotation.
Congenital peritoneal fibrous bands (Ladd bands) fix the abnormally positioned cecum to the right posterior abdominal wall, crossing and compressing the descending duodenum.
Incomplete duodenal recanalization produces an intraluminal duodenal web with the windsock sign: a thin mucosal membrane stretching distally into the third duodenum on contrast series.
Triple bubble sign indicates jejunal atresia caused by intrauterine vascular mesenteric accident; distal ileal atresia shows multiple dilated loops with air-fluid levels and microcolon.

lessonTopics.title: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis and Intussusception Imaging
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric GI & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis diagnostic ultrasound criteria: pyloric muscle wall thickness >= 3.0 mm (in transverse plane) and pyloric channel length >= 14-15 mm (mnemonic: pi = 3.14).
The elongated, thickened pylorus projecting into the fluid-filled gastric antrum mimics the uterine cervix (cervix sign / doughnut sign).
Barium upper GI demonstrates the string sign (elongated narrow pyloric canal), double-track sign (parallel mucosal streaks), and shoulder sign (muscle bulging into antrum).
Transverse abdominal ultrasound shows a multilayered concentric target or doughnut sign (diameter 3-5 cm), with alternating echogenic mucosa and hypoechoic edematous muscle walls.
Longitudinal ultrasound views of the intussusceptum telescoping into the intussuscipiens create the pseudokidney or sandwich sign.
Pneumatic reduction uses maximum safe pressure of 120 mmHg in infants, with success confirmed by free reflux of air into multiple small bowel loops.
Plain radiograph prior to reduction must exclude free intraperitoneal air (Rigler sign, falciform ligament sign) and clinical signs of peritonitis.
Ultrasound identifies pathological lead points (Meckel diverticulum, duplication cyst, inverted appendiceal stump, lymphoma) as focal cystic or solid masses within the intussusception head.

lessonTopics.title: Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC) and Neonatal Perforation
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric GI & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Pneumatosis intestinalis (intramural gas appearing as linear or bubbly radiolucencies in bowel wall) is the diagnostic hallmark of NEC (Bell stage IIA).
Portal venous gas manifests as branching, branching linear lucencies extending into the peripheral hepatic parenchyma on radiograph, differentiating from central biliary gas.
A fixed, unchanging, dilated bowel loop identified on sequential radiographs over 24-36 hours indicates full-thickness ischemia or impending perforation.
Left lateral decubitus or cross-table lateral views are essential to detect free peritoneal air collecting over the anterior or non-dependent liver surface.
Pneumoperitoneum produces the football sign (massive oval peritoneal air lucency outlined by parietal peritoneum) and Rigler sign (double-wall visualization of bowel).
High-frequency ultrasound demonstrates absent bowel wall blood flow by color Doppler (Y-sign / ring-down artifacts), predicting transmural bowel infarction.
Meconium ileus shows Neuhauser soap-bubble sign in the right iliac fossa with microcolon on contrast enema; meconium plug syndrome displays transient rectosigmoid cast relieved by contrast.

Ischemic post-NEC colonic strictures develop in 15-30% of surviving infants, located predominantly in the left colon (splenic flexure and sigmoid) requiring contrast enema evaluation prior to re-feeding.

lessonTopics.title: Anorectal Malformations and VACTERL Association
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric GI & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Krickenbeck classification categorizes anorectal malformations (ARM) by fistula presence: perineal, rectourethral (bulbar/prostatic), rectovesical, vestibular, and persistent cloaca.
Prone cross-table lateral (or invertogram) radiograph is performed at 18-24 hours of life to allow swallowed gas to reach the distal rectal pouch through meconium.
On lateral pelvic radiography, the pubococcygeal (PC) line connects the superior pubic bone to the sacrococcygeal junction; rectal gas ending below the ischial spine indicates a low malformation.
High-frequency perineal ultrasound accurately measures the distance from the blind rectal pouch to the perineal skin (pouch-perineum distance < 10 mm indicates low ARM amenable to primary repair).

Every infant with ARM mandates complete VACTERL screening: Vertebral anomalies (70%), Anal atresia, Cardiac defects (30-40%), Tracheoesophageal fistula (20%), Renal anomalies (50%), and Limb anomalies (radial ray).
Persistent cloaca in females features confluence of the urethra, vagina, and rectum into a single common perineal channel, requiring genitography and 3D pelvic MRI.
Spinal MRI or neonatal neurosonography is mandatory in all high/intermediate ARMs due to a 30-45% coexistence of occult spinal dysraphism and tethered cord.
The sacral ratio measured on lateral pelvic radiograph (< 0.74 normal, < 0.4 severely hypoplastic) correlates with sacral nerve root innervation and predicts long-term fecal continence.

modules.title: Pediatric Solid Abdominal Tumors: Neuroblastoma and Wilms Tumor

lessonTopics.title: Imaging Differentiation of Neuroblastoma and Wilms Tumor
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric Abdomen & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Neuroblastoma encases, drapes, and surrounds retroperitoneal great vessels (aorta, celiac, SMA) without vascular occlusion, extending across the midline behind the aorta.
Coarse, amorphous calcification is detected by CT in 80-90% and ultrasound in 50% of neuroblastomas, originating from adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain.
International Neuroblastoma Risk Group Staging System (INRGSS) stages L1 (localized without IDRFs), L2 (locoregional with one or more IDRFs), M (distant metastases), and MS (infants < 18 months).
Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) originates from the renal parenchyma, displacing normal parenchyma peripherally to create the classic claw sign (beak of parenchyma wrapping the tumor).
Wilms tumor displaces adjacent vessels rather than encasing them; calcification is rare (< 10-15%); high propensity for renal vein and IVC tumor thrombus extension (5-10%).
Nephroblastomatosis manifests as diffuse, subcapsular, wedge-shaped peripheral cortical nephrogenic rests with low T1 signal and minimal contrast enhancement compared to normal renal parenchyma.
Hepatoblastoma is the most common primary malignant liver tumor in infants < 3 years, presenting as a solitary large, heterogeneous vascular mass with calcifications in 50% and marked AFP elevation.
Congenital mesoblastic nephroma is the most common renal neoplasm in neonates (< 3 months); cellular subtype harbors ETV6-NTRK3 gene fusion, indistinguishable from Wilms by imaging alone.

modules.title: Congenital Hydronephrosis, VUR and Posterior Urethral Valves

lessonTopics.title: Antenatal Hydronephrosis, VCUG Grading and Posterior Urethral Valves
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric GU & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: The multidisciplinary Urinary Tract Dilation (UTD) classification grades postnatal hydronephrosis into UTD P1 (low risk), P2 (intermediate risk), and P3 (high risk with parenchymal thinning).
Initial postnatal renal ultrasound for antenatal hydronephrosis is scheduled after 48-72 hours of life to avoid underestimating severity due to transient neonatal oliguria.

mustKnow.term: VCUG reflux grading I to V
mustKnow.fact: International Reflux Study grading: Grade I (ureter only), Grade II (pelvis without dilatation), Grade III (mild dilatation/blunting), Grade IV (moderate tortuosity), Grade V (gross hydroureteronephrosis and tortuosity).
Antenatal ultrasound displays the keyhole sign: a distended thick-walled urinary bladder with dilated posterior urethra; oligohydramnios and bilateral hydroureteronephrosis.
VCUG demonstrates abrupt caliber change with dilated, elongated posterior urethra and prominent hypertrophied bladder neck with trabeculated bladder wall during voiding.
UPJ obstruction is the most common cause of congenital hydronephrosis, showing marked renal pelvicalyceal dilatation with an abrupt transition to a normal non-dilated ureter.

Technetium-99m MAG3 diuretic renogram assesses functional obstruction: clearance half-time (T1/2) < 10 min is non-obstructed, 10-20 min indeterminate, and > 20 min indicates significant mechanical obstruction.

MCDK features multiple non-communicating cysts of varying sizes separated by echogenic dysplastic stroma, absence of normal renal parenchyma, and atretic non-visualized ureter; contralateral VUR in 20-30%.

modules.title: Non-Accidental Trauma, Salter-Harris Fractures and Bone Infections

lessonTopics.title: Non-Accidental Trauma (NAT): High-Specificity Skeletal Lesions
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric MSK & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Classic metaphyseal lesions (CML / corner fracture / bucket-handle fracture) have highest specificity for physical abuse in infants, caused by planar shearing forces during violent shaking or flailing.
mustKnow.source: ACR Appropriateness Criteria for Child Abuse

mustKnow.fact: Posterior rib fractures located adjacent to the costovertebral articulation result from forceful anteroposterior thoracic compression during manual squeezing of an infant.
Full radiographic skeletal survey (minimum 21 dedicated high-detail views) is mandatory for any child under 2 years with suspected physical abuse.
Repeat skeletal survey at 10-14 days detects subtle occult fractures that become visible through subperiosteal new bone formation and callus remodeling.

Salter-Harris: Type I (Slipped physis), Type II (Above physis into metaphysis, 75% most common, Thurston Holland fragment), Type III (Lower into epiphysis), Type IV (Through metaphysis and epiphysis), Type V (Rammed / crush).
Toddler fracture is an accidental, non-displaced spiral or oblique fracture of the distal tibial shaft in ambulatory children aged 9 months to 3 years, presenting with refusal to bear weight.
MRI is the most sensitive imaging modality for pediatric osteomyelitis (> 95%), demonstrating replacement of normal fatty marrow with low T1 signal, high T2/STIR edema, and subperiosteal abscess.
Hip ultrasonography detects joint effusion as capsular distension > 2 mm compared to asymptomatic contralateral hip; ultrasound-guided joint aspiration confirms infection.

lessonTopics.title: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip and Common Skeletal Dysplasias
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric MSK & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Graf ultrasound method: alpha angle (bone acetabular roof) >= 60 degrees indicates mature Type 1 hip; beta angle (cartilage roof) < 55 degrees; alpha < 50 degrees indicates significant dysplasia.
Normal static ultrasound demonstrates at least 50% of the cartilaginous femoral head seated within the bony acetabular fossa.
On pelvic radiographs after 4-6 months: normal femoral head ossification center lies in the inferomedial quadrant formed by horizontal Hilgenreiner and vertical Perkin lines.
Acetabular index angle should normally measure < 30 degrees at birth and declines to < 20 degrees by 2 years; angles > 30 degrees indicate acetabular dysplasia.
Achondroplasia (FGFR3 mutation) features progressive narrowing of interpediculate distances caudally in lumbar spine, tombstone iliac wings, horizontal flat acetabular roofs, and trident hands.
Thanatophoric dysplasia (lethal FGFR3 mutation) displays telephone receiver-curved femurs (Type 1) or cloverleaf skull / kleeblattschadel with straighter femurs (Type 2), with severe platyspondyly.

Type II perinatal lethal osteogenesis imperfecta (COL1A1/COL1A2) features accordion-pleated crumpling of long bones, innumerable rib fractures with beading, and defective calvarial ossification (wormian bones).
Nutritional and metabolic rickets produces cupping, fraying, splaying, and widening of the radiolucent physeal zone at rapidly growing metaphyses (wrist and knee).

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Bone Tumors: Osteosarcoma, Ewing Sarcoma and LCH
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric MSK & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Conventional osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant bone tumor in children/adolescents (peak age 10-20 years), located in the metaphysis of long bones (distal femur 45%, proximal tibia 20%).
Classic radiograph shows cloud-like or cumulus osteoid matrix calcification, cortical destruction, sunburst periosteal reaction, and Codman triangle.
Ewing sarcoma (EWSR1-FLI1 translocation, t(11;22)) characteristically affects the diaphysis or metadiaphysis of long bones and pelvis, showing permeative 'moth-eaten' bone destruction.
Multilayered concentric lamellated subperiosteal new bone formation (onion-skin appearance) accompanied by a massive disproportionate soft-tissue mass is classic for Ewing sarcoma.
LCH / eosinophilic granuloma of bone causes punched-out osteolytic lesions without sclerotic margins in the skull (beveled-edge sign) and vertebra plana (pancake vertebra) in the spine.
ABC is an expansile, eccentric lytic metaphyseal lesion with internal bony septations, demonstrating pathognomonic multiple fluid-fluid levels on T2-weighted MRI.
NOF (fibrous cortical defect when < 2 cm) is a benign, eccentric, multilocular lytic lesion with a scalloped, sclerotic border in the posterior distal femoral or proximal tibial metaphysis.
Osteochondroma (exostosis) demonstrates absolute pathognomonic continuity of its cortical and medullary cavity with that of the underlying parent bone, pointing away from the nearest joint.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Hip Pathology: SCFE, Legg-Calve-Perthes and Synovitis
lessonTopics.bookChapter: Crack the Core: Pediatric MSK & RDN11

mustKnow.fact: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) is a Type I Salter-Harris physeal fracture occurring in overweight adolescents (males 12-14 years, females 10-12 years), presenting with knee/thigh pain.

On AP frog-leg lateral pelvic radiograph, Klein line drawn along the superior border of the femoral neck normally intersects the lateral epiphysis; failure to intersect defines Trethowan sign of SCFE.
The femoral neck displaces anterosuperiorly while the capital femoral epiphysis slips posteromedially into the acetabulum (ice cream falling off the cone appearance).
Bilateral SCFE occurs in 20-40% of patients (up to 50% in underlying endocrinopathy: hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency), mandating prophylactic pinning of the contralateral hip.
LCPD is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis occurring in active boys aged 4 to 8 years (4:1 male ratio), presenting with an unprovoked, painless limp.
Perthes disease progresses through four radiographic stages: Stage 1 Initial (crescent sign / subchondral fracture), Stage 2 Fragmentation, Stage 3 Reossification, and Stage 4 Remodeling/healed.
Herring lateral pillar classification on AP pelvis: Group A (100% lateral pillar height maintained), Group B (> 50% height), and Group C (< 50% height, poor long-term prognosis).
Transient synovitis (toxic synovitis) is a benign, self-limiting post-viral inflammatory hip effusion in children aged 3-8 years; normal radiograph, effusion resolves spontaneously within 7-10 days.
